body_markdown:
Consumer watchdog Which? raises concerns after five popular rapid testing kits produce conflicting readings, leaving questions over reliability, safety and value for money.


At-home health testing kits promise a quick and convenient way to check important aspects of your health without having to book a GP appointment or visit a laboratory. However, a new investigation has raised serious questions about the reliability of popular vitamin D self-test kits, with several products producing results that differed significantly from a professional laboratory test.


Consumer watchdog Which? tested five widely available rapid vitamin D testing kits and discovered considerable variations in their results. The findings have prompted concerns that consumers could be receiving misleading information about their vitamin D levels, potentially leading to unnecessary worry, false reassurance or inappropriate supplement use.


## Five Popular Vitamin D Tests Put to the Test


Which? purchased five rapid vitamin D self-testing kits from well-known retailers and healthcare brands. The products included tests from Boots, Berkeley Health, MyHealthChecked, OneStep and Newfoundland Diagnostics.


Each kit cost approximately £8, making them an affordable option for people looking to monitor their vitamin D levels from home.


To assess their performance, the watchdog compared the results against a laboratory blood test carried out on the same day. The laboratory was registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), and its findings showed that the tested individual's vitamin D levels were within the sufficient range.


However, the rapid home tests delivered a very different picture.


Results from MyHealthChecked and OneStep suggested that vitamin D levels were insufficient, while Newfoundland and Berkeley Health indicated deficient levels.


The investigation highlighted how the same person's blood sample could produce very different interpretations depending on which home testing kit was used.


## Why Are the Results So Different?


One important factor behind the discrepancies is the threshold used to determine whether someone has sufficient vitamin D.


Generally, a vitamin D reading above 50 nmol/L is considered sufficient. However, some rapid self-testing kits use a higher threshold of 75 nmol/L.


This difference can have a significant impact on how results are interpreted.


Someone whose vitamin D level falls between these two figures could be considered sufficient under one measurement standard but insufficient under another.


This means consumers may receive a result suggesting they have low vitamin D levels even when a laboratory test indicates otherwise.


Although different testing methods and clinical thresholds can influence results, Which? raised concerns about the extent of the variation identified during its investigation.


## The Hidden Risks of Unreliable Home Health Checks


The biggest concern is not simply that a home test might produce an inaccurate reading. It is what consumers might do after receiving that result.


People who are incorrectly told they have low vitamin D levels may become unnecessarily anxious or spend money on supplements they do not need.


Some could even start taking high-dose vitamin D supplements without seeking professional advice.


Taking excessive amounts of vitamin D over time can cause a build-up of calcium in the body, potentially leading to kidney damage and other health complications.


On the other hand, a misleading result suggesting that vitamin D levels are normal could provide false reassurance to someone who actually needs further investigation.


This is particularly concerning for people who rely on home testing because they want to take greater control of their health.


## Which? Calls for Better Standards


Following the investigation, Which? shared its findings with the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).


The regulator confirmed that it was reviewing existing regulations, with proposed changes intended to improve standards for self-testing products.


Sue Davies, head of consumer rights and food policy at Which?, said consumers turn to home health checks for reassurance and as a convenient way to manage their wellbeing.


She warned that it was deeply concerning that products sold by major high street retailers and online providers had produced contradictory results.


The watchdog believes consumers should be able to trust the information provided by health testing products, particularly when those results could influence decisions about their wellbeing.


## What Have the Brands Said?


The companies involved have responded to the concerns raised by the investigation.


Boots and MyHealthChecked said their rapid self-test kits provide customers with a convenient screening option and comply with relevant regulatory requirements.


They also highlighted the support available through pharmacy teams, who can help customers understand their results, assess whether self-testing is suitable and decide whether further advice from a GP may be appropriate.


Newfoundland Diagnostics said its performance data formed part of a wider body of evidence considered during regulatory assessment.


Meanwhile, Berkeley Health maintained that the clinical evidence supporting its tests was sufficient to meet the compliance requirements for CE marking.


The responses highlight the importance of understanding the difference between regulatory compliance and the ability of a particular test to provide results that closely match a laboratory measurement.


## Should You Trust At-Home Vitamin D Tests?


Home testing kits can offer convenience, but consumers should be cautious about treating their results as a definitive diagnosis.


A rapid self-test is generally intended to provide an indication of a possible health issue rather than replace professional medical assessment.


Anyone concerned about their vitamin D levels should consider speaking to a qualified healthcare professional, particularly before starting high-dose supplements or making significant changes to their diet.


A GP can assess individual circumstances and advise whether a laboratory blood test or further investigation is appropriate.


It is also important to remember that vitamin D requirements can vary depending on age, lifestyle, health circumstances and other individual factors.


## What Happens Next?


The investigation has renewed questions about whether current regulations provide sufficient protection for people purchasing self-testing products.


Under existing requirements, rapid self-tests must be registered with the MHRA as diagnostic devices and meet applicable in vitro diagnostic regulatory requirements.


However, Which?'s findings suggest that further improvements may be needed to help consumers make informed decisions when purchasing health testing kits.


As demand for convenient home healthcare continues to grow, reliability and transparency will remain essential.


For now, the message is clear: a quick result does not always mean an accurate one. Before spending money on a home vitamin D test or changing your supplement routine, it is worth seeking professional advice.


**DISCLAIMER:** This article is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is not intended to provide medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Home testing kits may produce results that require professional interpretation. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional about concerns relating to vitamin D levels, testing or supplementation. Do not start high-dose supplements based solely on a home test result.
